parsed.explanation: The combined regime imposes genuine tier-1 universal exposures on the traveller rather than resident-only gaps: a screening directive to refuse cases where documents or records cast doubt on an applicant's sex (with a possible, non-automatic lifetime fraud finding), an entry ban on trans athletes, and a division law making restroom/changing-room use in government buildings AND public-facing private businesses — hospitals, restaurants, gas stations, venues — a misdemeanour carrying up to a year. Documented custody conditions (hormone removal, forced labour, sexual abuse, a bathroom arrestee held in a men's ward) set the severity of what follows an outing high. Mitigating: no documented enforcement against visitors, no trans-specific violence data above baseline, a national gender-identity hate-crime statute, active litigation, and a 16 June 2026 narrowing whose status is unresolved. Rate materially below administrative-friction anchors, and above the execution-tier extremes.

entry_documents.exposure: National cable directs officers to refuse where documents/records show discrepancy or reasonable doubt as to sex, adds a case-note tag, and flags possible (non-automatic) lifetime ineligibility under the fraud ground; trans-athlete entry ban; at least eight governments issued advisories after detentions.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiry; the visitor's home-issued document governs; passport restrictions are under national court challenge; a legal-aid FAQ explains documentation options.
entry_documents.interaction: A division-issued ID retaining an X marker that diverges from a passport M/F marker manufactures exactly the discrepancy the cable targets, escalating a port stop into a misrepresentation inquiry.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National corrections policies mandate haircutting, hormone removal and psychiatric substitution for trans inmates; immigration detainees report forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse; a bathroom arrestee was held 24 hours in a men's ward.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: A September 2024 national ruling nullified a state law barring prisoner hormone therapy; several executive measures are enjoined; litigation ongoing.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A facilities arrest in the division flows into exactly this custody system, where placement follows birth sex and documented harm recurs.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Division law (effective 1 July 2026) criminalises restroom/changing-room use not matching birth sex in government buildings and all public-facing private businesses — hospitals, restaurants, venues, gas stations — first offence up to a year; nationally 4 states criminalise in some circumstances and one capitol arrest was recorded.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Suit filed 30 April 2026 on due-process, equal-protection and privacy grounds; a reported 16 June 2026 narrowing (status unresolved); statutory exemptions for assistance, emergency and custodial purposes; many states have no ban.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Because hospitals and hospitality are covered, ordinary travel — eating, refuelling, emergency care — carries the exposure everywhere in the division, not just in civic buildings.

care_services.exposure: Hospitals are covered private businesses under the division's facility law, so restroom use during treatment is criminalised; national measures target gender-affirming care for minors and would bar public reimbursement under 18.
care_services.protection: Not documented. No traveller-facing care protection or clinical non-discrimination guarantee for visitors is documented.
care_services.interaction: An emergency or injury outs the traveller to medics and simultaneously places her inside a facility whose restrooms carry criminal exposure.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: The May 2026 counterterrorism strategy names 'radically pro-transgender' groups for rapid identification and neutralisation; a DOJ reward memorandum uses 'radical gender ideology'; official rhetoric frames trans advocacy as extremist.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The strategy states powers will not target mere disagreement; national hate-crime statute covers gender identity; 22 states plus the capital district outlaw gender-identity discrimination.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: Rhetoric raises the odds that police contact over a facilities complaint is read through a security lens rather than as a civil matter.

minors_guardians.exposure: A March 2026 division law requires schools, childcare providers and medical professionals to disclose a trans minor's status to parents within three days; schools may not use pronouns inconsistent with birth certificates; the facility criminalisation reaches minors; national order directs prosecution of teachers facilitating social transition.
minors_guardians.protection: Parental-consent, emancipation and court-order routes for minors' care; pending litigation; municipal ordinances cover about 40% of the division's population.
minors_guardians.interaction: A guardian travelling with a trans minor faces forced disclosure to institutions plus the minor's own facility exposure, and a hospital visit triggers both.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: A documented restroom arrest with handcuffing and men's-ward detention shows police acting on the facility law; no division-specific trans violence data materially above the general homicide rate was identified.
street_violence_police_response.protection: National gender-identity hate-crime statute; 23 states cover gender identity in bias-crime statutes; an active civil-liberties organisation litigates and publicises.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Reporting a harassment incident may itself expose the traveller's documents to officers empowered to act on the facility law.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Whether the reported 16 June 2026 narrowing survives, the outcome of the April 2026 suit, and the current status of the birth-certificate law are unresolved; no enforcement action against a visitor was identified, so visitor-facing practice is untested.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Functioning courts and active constitutional litigation; legal-aid FAQ; injunctions have blocked several national measures.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Paper protections here run through courts that are simultaneously the enforcement forum for the hostile facility rule, so relief is slow and provisional.

anchor_checks.comparison: That anchor ends in a logged discrepancy and delay, with a charter expressly barring prolonged holds and no criminal statute. Here a criminal facility statute reaching every restaurant and hospital, plus a screening directive to refuse on sex doubt, means the traveller carries exposure that resolves in custody rather than a logged stop. Lower than that anchor.

That anchor is service denial at a hostel with a patrol officer declining to detain. Here refusal is not the worst outcome: detention and prosecution are authorized for ordinary facility use, and documented custody conditions include hormone removal and abuse. Materially lower than that anchor.

That anchor has a charter requiring acceptance of self-declared markers, breached only by an awkward inspector before a supervisor corrects it. Here the operative national rule runs the other way — doubt as to sex is a refusal trigger — and the division criminalises facilities. Far below that anchor.

parsed.synthesis: The visitor meets two layered universal exposures: a screening regime that treats document or sex doubt as a refusal trigger (with a latent lifetime fraud finding), and a division statute criminalising restroom use in all public-facing private businesses with a year's exposure. Neither is contingent on the traveller's conduct beyond being read as trans. What follows an outing is severe: documented hormone removal, forced labour and sexual abuse in custody, and birth-sex facility placement. Offsetting factors are real but partial — a national hate-crime statute, active constitutional litigation, and no documented enforcement against visitors — and courts here are also the enforcement forum for the hostile rule, so relief is provisional. The rating sits in the High Risk band, below jurisdictions where hostile law is unenforced and above the execution-tier extremes.
